opener: A prefabricated office cabin is an office built as numbered steel panels, bolted together on a module grid rather than welded shut in one piece. Panels arrive on a transport break seam, bolt up at spline joints, and can be unbolted again when the site closes, so the same cabin moves to the next project or joins a neighbour through a site joining strip to form a multi-bay office. It is bought by project buyers, layout planners and installation crews who expect the office to be dismantled, extended or relocated inside its working life. Six approved sizes run from 10×10 ft at 100 sq ft to 40×10 ft at 400 sq ft, each with its own general arrangement drawing, opening schedule and staged desk count, priced ex-GST for the office module framework.

descriptionHtml:
Prefabricated office cabin or prefab office building?

Two quite different things are searched for with the words prefabricated office. The first is a prefabricated office building: a steel-frame structure erected on a foundation, sized in thousands of square feet, competing with conventional construction. The second is a prefabricated office cabin: a finished steel room of 100 to 400 square feet that arrives on a trailer, is set on supports and is working the same day. This page is the second thing only, and every figure below describes a cabin.

If a foundation, a design team and a building permit are already part of the plan, the Prefab Buildings and Pre-Engineered Buildings ranges are where that requirement belongs. If the office has to exist on ground that will be handed back, or has to follow a project from one alignment to the next, a cabin is the right instrument and the whole page applies.

The word prefabricated does a second job here that portable does not. Every steel cabin SAMAN builds is portable, because it lifts and travels. Only some are prefabricated in the strict sense of being assembled on site from separately manufactured panels. That distinction is the reason this page exists as its own product rather than as a synonym of the Portable Office Cabin hub, and it is what the next section describes.

What makes a cabin prefabricated rather than portable

A readymade office cabin leaves the works as one welded box. The frame is welded, the sheets are fixed to the frame, the interior is finished inside the finished shell, and the unit is craned onto a trailer complete. It is a good product and it is the cheaper of the two, because welding a shell once is less work than detailing a shell that must come apart.

A prefabricated office cabin is drawn the other way round. The shell is set out on a module grid datum, and the walls, roof and floor are made as separately numbered panels that meet at bolted spline joints. A transport break seam is drawn where the shell is intended to divide. Corner interface plates locate the panels against each other, and a site joining strip closes the junction between one module and the next.

The consequences are practical rather than theoretical. A panel that is bolted can be unbolted, so the cabin can be taken down, stacked flat and re-erected rather than being craned whole down a road that may not take it. A junction that is drawn can be repeated, so a second module can be brought against the first later without cutting either shell. A numbered panel can be replaced, so a wall damaged by a reversing truck is a panel swap and not a fabrication job on a live site.

None of that removes the crane from the first delivery. These cabins are still lifted by four corner eye plates, one at each top corner, and still travel on an open trailer. What changes is what happens after the first placement, which is the part of the cost a project buyer usually meets twice.

Prefabricated, readymade or small: which page you need

SAMAN publishes three office cabin pages that a buyer can reasonably confuse, and the six sizes on this page appear on two of them. The difference is not the size ladder; it is the construction and the price rule.

The Readymade Office Cabin range carries the same six sizes as welded units at a base rate of ₹1,250 per sq ft at 200 sq ft. Buy from that page when the office is going to one place and staying there, when the budget matters more than the second move, and when nobody expects to add a bay.

This page carries the same six sizes as bolted panel modules at ₹1,300 per sq ft at 200 sq ft, roughly four per cent more. Buy from this page when the office is expected to be dismantled, relocated or extended, when the site has an access route that argues for delivering a shell in pieces, or when a multi-bay run is already on the drawing board.

The Small Office Cabin page is a different question again. It starts at 8×6 ft and 48 square feet and covers the one-person and two-person rooms this page does not publish at all. If the whole requirement is a gate clerk or a single supervisor, that page is cheaper and better fitted. This page starts at 100 square feet because a panel module below that size costs more to detail than it saves.

Container Offices sit outside all three. A container office is built from or like an ISO shipping container, with corner castings and a container frame. Nothing on this page is a container: the base is a plain steel skid and the corner fitting is a compact one-hole lifting eye plate. If a container shell is what is wanted, the Container Offices range is the right cluster.

How to choose between 100 and 400 square feet

Start from the number of people who sit inside on an ordinary working day, then check what the plot allows, then read the opening schedule to confirm the walls suit the fit-out.

One to four people at fixed desks fit the 10×10 ft at 100 square feet. Three people on ground that is long and narrow fit the 20×8 ft, which is the only 8 ft body on the page and the only one-way roof. A team of five with a manager who needs a door takes the 20×10 ft, and the 20×12 ft is the same plan for the same team where the circulation in a 10 ft body is too tight. Twelve people in one undivided room take the 30×10 ft. Eight people plus two managers who each need their own room take the 40×10 ft.

The opening schedule matters more than it looks. The 10×10 ft is the only size whose entrance wall carries no window at all, which makes it the easiest size to line with boards, racking or a switchboard. Every other size puts a window either side of the door on the entrance wall, which is better for daylight and worse for wall-mounted equipment. The two largest sizes carry two external doors rather than one, which is what allows a twelve-desk room and a package office to be evacuated sensibly.

The table below is every published size with the facts that decide between them. Prices are ex-GST for the module framework; the GST-inclusive figure for each size is shown on the size selector above.

What the bolted joint changes on your site

Four details on the general arrangement drawings are what a site actually handles, and each of them is drawn before production rather than resolved on site.

The module grid datum is the line everything else is measured from. It is why a second module can be set against the first years later and still meet it squarely, and it is why the opening positions on this page are published as coordinates from End C rather than as a description.

The bolted spline joint is the junction between two panels. It is designed to be opened, which is a different requirement from a joint that only has to be closed once, and it is the reason the panel schedule and the panel numbering exist as a document handed over with the cabin.

The transport break seam is where the shell is intended to divide for a road move. Knowing where it is before the first delivery is what turns a second move from an improvisation into a planned operation.

The site joining strip closes the gap when two modules stand side by side. It is the same detail on all six sizes, which is the whole reason a 20×10 ft office bought this year can grow into a two-bay office next year rather than being replaced.

  • Module grid datum: every opening on this page is dimensioned from End C, so a later bay meets the first squarely
  • Bolted spline joint: panel junctions are designed to be opened, not only closed once
  • Transport break seam: the shell divides where the drawing says, so a second move is planned rather than improvised
  • Site joining strip: the same junction detail on all six sizes, which is what lets one module become two bays
  • Corner interface plates and panel numbering: a damaged wall is a panel swap, not fabrication on a live site

Roof, lifting and transport across the six sizes

Five of the six sizes carry a centred ridge running the full length of the cabin, with two planes falling across the width and a ridge rise of only five to six inches above each eave. The roof reads almost level and is drawn that way deliberately: a shallow fall keeps the transport height down and keeps the panel run above the eaves uninterrupted, which matters on a shell that is meant to come apart.

The 20×8 ft is the exception. Its roof is a single one-way plane falling across the 8 ft width with the same five to six inches of total fall, no ridge, and straight eaves on both long walls. On a body only eight feet wide a ridge would buy nothing and would complicate the panel run.

Lifting is identical across all six. Four compact one-hole eye plates sit at the four top corners, H1 to H4, and nowhere else. There is no mid-span hook and no ridge hook, and there are no ISO corner castings, because these are not container-derived units. Every size is 8.5 ft nominal in height, which is what keeps the loaded trailer inside normal road clearances.

What the price covers and what is quoted separately

The published price is the office module framework in the approved size, with its drawn openings, its internal finish and its electrical provision as scheduled on the general arrangement drawing. It is quoted ex-GST; 18 per cent GST is added at invoice and both figures are shown on the size selector.

The price rule is arithmetic, not negotiation. A base rate of ₹1,300 per square foot applies at 200 square feet. Below that, smaller areas carry a band uplift because the fixed content of a cabin does not shrink with its floor: 100 to 149 square feet adds 15 per cent, 150 to 199 adds 10 per cent. Above 200, larger areas take a band reduction: 201 to 300 takes 4 per cent off, 301 to 400 takes 5 per cent off. That is where each of the six rates on this page comes from and it can be checked against the area in the table above.

What is not in the price is stated rather than implied. Craneage and offloading at your site, joining two or more modules together, any sanitary or plumbing fit-out, special performance evidence such as certified test data for a particular exposure, and multi-unit integration works are quotation items. Site preparation, the supporting pad and the incoming electrical supply are the buyer's scope.

Warranty period and exclusions are confirmed in the final quotation for your order. The general arrangement drawings on this page are buyer-facing control drawings and are marked not for fabrication: approved shop drawings, project engineering, the final load schedule and the signed quotation govern what is built.

Frequently asked questions about prefab office cabins

Yes. All six sizes carry the same corner interface plates and site joining strip, so a second module can be brought against the first and closed at the junction. Multi-unit integration is a quotation item, not part of the published price.

Is a prefabricated office cabin the same as a container office?

No. A container office is built from or like an ISO shipping container with corner castings. These cabins sit on a plain steel skid and use compact one-hole lifting eye plates. Container-derived offices are on the Container Offices pages.

applicationsContent.h2: Compare the Six Prefabricated Office Cabin Sizes and Prices
applicationsContent.intro: Six approved sizes, one bolted panel platform, one price rule. Each shows its GA drawing, its opening schedule and its staged desks.

panels.h3: 10×10 ft Prefabricated Office Cabin: 100 sq ft, Four Desks
panels.paragraph: The smallest module on the panel platform and the only one whose entrance wall carries no glazing at all. Wall A is a door and nothing else, which leaves three solid panel runs a fit-out can use for a board, a switchboard or shelving without working around a window head. Buy it as the repeatable unit: a gate office, a stores office or a supervisor's room that will be unbolted and moved when the phase ends. Four desks are staged in the drawing; the price is for the module framework.
applications: Rate ₹1,495 per sq ft: the 100–149 sq ft band adds 15% to the ₹1,300 base
1 external door on Wall A at 3.5–6.5 ft; no window on the entrance wall
3 windows, one each on Wall B, End C and End D, all centred on their wall
4 desks staged, no partition; centred-ridge roof, 5–6 in rise across 10 ft
Presentation colours: slate navy outside, champagne cream inside

image.alt: GA board for the 10x10 ft prefabricated office cabin: plan with four staged desks, Wall A door-only elevation and one centred window on each of the other three walls

panels.h3: 20×8 ft Prefabricated Office Cabin: 160 sq ft on Narrow Ground
panels.paragraph: The only one-way roof in the set, and the size to choose when the plot has length but no depth. An 8 ft body clears a narrow gate and sits along a boundary strip where a 10 ft module will not, and the roof sheds across the width in a single plane with no ridge, so the panel run above the eaves stays uninterrupted. Three desks work in a single open bay with the door landing centrally between two window pairs. Nothing is partitioned, so the whole 160 sq ft reads as one room.
applications: Rate ₹1,430 per sq ft: the 150–199 sq ft band adds 10% to the ₹1,300 base
Wall A from End C: window 1.5–5.5 ft, door 8.5–11.5 ft, window 14.5–18.5 ft
Wall B carries two windows at 1.5–5.5 ft and 14.5–18.5 ft; both ends centred
One-way roof, 5–6 in total fall across the 8 ft width, no ridge, no long fall
3 desks staged, open plan, no partition; premium taupe outside, sage grey inside

image.alt: GA board for the 20x8 ft prefabricated office cabin: open plan with three staged desks, window-door-window on Wall A and the one-way roof orientation

panels.h3: 20×10 ft Prefabricated Office Cabin: Manager Room Plus Five
panels.paragraph: The reference module of the platform and the size the base rate is set on. A full-width partition at 11 ft 10 in from End C splits the shell into an 11 ft 10 in team zone and an 8 ft 2 in manager room, with a 2 ft 6 in internal door centred on the aisle so the two zones share one circulation line. Three desks sit along Wall B under a run of three ceiling-fixed cabinet modules and two along Wall A. The manager room takes a desk and two guest chairs and is served by the far window pair.
applications: Rate ₹1,300 per sq ft: this is the 200 sq ft base, no band adjustment applied
Wall A from End C: window 1.5–5.5 ft, door 8.5–11.5 ft, window 14.5–18.5 ft
Wall B carries two windows at 1.5–5.5 ft and 14.5–18.5 ft; both ends centred
Partition P1 at 11 ft 10 in with a 2 ft 6 in centred internal door, no partition glazing
5 team desks, three on Wall B and two on Wall A, plus manager desk and two guest chairs

image.alt: GA board for the 20x10 ft prefabricated office cabin: team zone and manager room split by partition P1 at 11 ft 10 in, with the six-window opening schedule

panels.h3: 20×12 ft Prefabricated Office Cabin: the Same Plan, 2 ft Wider
panels.paragraph: A deliberate derivative rather than a new plan. It keeps the 20×10 longitudinal ledger unchanged, the same partition at 11 ft 10 in, the same five team desks and the same manager set, and spends the extra two feet entirely on clear width. That produces a continuous 2 ft strip down the length: a chair pushes back from a Wall B desk without blocking the aisle, and two people pass behind a seated colleague. Choose it when the seat count is right but the circulation in a 10 ft body is not.
applications: Rate ₹1,248 per sq ft: the 201–300 sq ft band takes 4% off the ₹1,300 base
Openings identical to the 20×10 on both long walls; end windows sit in the 4–8 ft span

panels.h3: 30×10 ft Prefabricated Office Cabin: 12 Desks, Two Doors
panels.paragraph: The maximum-capacity open plan. Nothing is partitioned across 300 sq ft, so the seat count rises to twelve, seven along Wall B and five along Wall A, and two external doors near the opposite ends give the room two ways out instead of one bottleneck at the middle. Wall B carries four windows to daylight the longer desk run; Wall A takes two, sitting between the doors. Buy it as a drawing office, a billing hall or a survey team room where the whole point is one undivided floor.

panels.paragraph: The largest module published here, and the only one drawn with two partitions. P1 lands at 8 ft 2 in and P2 at 31 ft 10 in from End C, cutting a manager room off each end and leaving a common office of eight desks between them, five along Wall B and three along Wall A. Each manager room keeps its own window pair and its own internal door near Wall A, so neither manager walks through the other's room. Two external doors serve the common office. It is a package-office plan, not a scaled-up 20×10.
